title: North America today
hook: Sikhs farm, drive, teach, heal and lead across Canada and the US

segments.voice: Yesterday, pardes, and your line was moved twice. Did you hear someone's second move? Today, the people on your street, or the next one over. Day one thousand thirty-three.

Five in the morning on an interstate. A long-haul truck pulls into a rest stop, and the driver, in a neat turban, stretches and heads for coffee. A few hours later, in a valley full of orchards, a farmer checks the peach trees. In a classroom, a teacher writes the day's date on the board. In a hospital, a nurse takes a pulse. In a city council chamber, a member stands to speak. Each of them is a Sikh, and the people they pass may not think about that at all. They may just think: that's my driver, my farmer, my kid's teacher, my nurse. Today is about the plain word for that.
screen: `A TRUCK AT A REST STOP.` → `ORCHARDS, CLASSROOMS, WARDS.` → `MY DRIVER, MY TEACHER, MY NURSE.`

segments.voice: First, the work. Across Canada and the United States, Sikhs farm, drive trucks and taxis, run shops, teach, heal and serve in public office. Some families have been here for generations, and some arrived last year. Second, the teaching under the work. The Sikh way calls this kirat karni, earning by honest work. Among the saloks at Ang 1376 of the Guru Granth Sahib, Namdev, a calico printer by trade, tells his friend Trilochan: with your hands and feet, do all your work, and keep your mind with the Pure One. Hands busy, mind with God, in one line. A paycheck isn't separate from the spiritual life; it's one of its places. Third, the open door. Beside honest work, the Sikh way asks for vand chakna, sharing what you earn. Gurdwaras across the continent serve langar to anyone who walks in. Sikh volunteers have cooked for neighbors after storms and fires, and handed out meals in parking lots and stadiums. Nobody is asked what they believe before they eat. Fourth, the word. Nobody is handed the title neighbor. It grows slowly, from showing up: the driver who waves at the same diner every week, the farmer who lends a ladder over the fence, the nurse who remembers your mother's name. That is today's line: neighbors. Sikhs in North America live it in ordinary ways, at the next desk, the next farm, the next house.
screen: `FARM, DRIVE, TEACH, HEAL, LEAD.` · `ANG 1376: HANDS AT WORK, MIND WITH GOD.` · `LANGAR FOR WHOEVER WALKS IN.` · `NEIGHBORS, MADE BY SHOWING UP.` · then, large: `NEIGHBORS.`

segments.voice: Two minutes with your neighbors. Sit, and let your breathing settle. Picture the people around where you live or work: the one next door, the one across the hall, the driver, the cashier, the person who fixes things. Choose one whose name you know, or whose face you know without a name. Breathe in, and see them clearly. Breathe out, and thank them silently for one thing they do that makes your days easier. If you pray, you can say Waheguru on each breath out. The bell holds the time.
Kirat. Honest work, lived out by Sikhs who farm, drive, teach, heal and lead across Canada and the US today. Today's word.
Your line: neighbors. Today, thank one neighbor out loud for something small, by name if you know it, and learn the name if you don't. Day one thousand thirty-three.

what a scholar hears: kirat karni and vand chakna set daily work and sharing at the center; at Ang 1376, Namdev, a bhagat whose words sit in the Guru Granth Sahib, puts hands at work and the mind with God in one line.
